Here's the super tl;dr from my perspective. Being transgender is a very simple matter of needing your body's sexual characteristics to align with being male, female, or, more rarely, neither/both.

Separate from that is the social construct of gender, created by society, which is the site of substantial interplay, controversy, and struggle, but also of many enriching experiences for many people. For example, you may have noticed that many cisgender men work fairly hard to embody masculinity, and it's not surprising that what's considered normative behavior for cisgender men is often normative for transgender men too. If many of the men you respect, admire, or compete with build impressive muscles and feel most attractive with a bit of stubble, it's not unusual for you to want to do the same for similar reasons.

I actually think you're right, on a technical level, that transgender individuals who conform to normative gender reinforce gender norms, but so do the vast majority of non-transgender individuals, in the same way, to a greater or equal extent, and for the same reasons: simple imitation, role modeling, and group dynamics. To take a trivial example, I didn't really wear makeup until it became normative in my social group and friends started planning outings to a popular beauty lab, but when we went there, of course I wanted my own carefully selected shade, and when my close friends take out their little tubes, I take out mine.

But what does this actually mean? We're reinforcing associations between femininity and makeup, but are we advancing a philosophical stance that women must or should wear makeup? We'd laugh that idea right out of existence. Yet of course the fact that we've chosen to wear makeup has some influence on women who know us and want to participate in this small but obviously gendered activity too. (We'd all be thrilled if one of our male friends joined us, but they don't seem to want to.)

Now, I'm certainly willing to concede that in this example I've reinforced a construct of femininity, along with my six non-trans friends who went to the beauty lab, including the woman who got us all into makeup and planned the trip. What I'm not sure is how I'm doing anything novel or different that non-trans women aren't already doing.

The reason I needed to be embodied in a female form is far more basic, though. It pertains more to biological sex. Beyond that, though, I don't engage with gender in particularly interesting ways. The things I want to do with my life, like writing books and maintaining an academic career and creating art, aren't really viewed as gender nonconforming anymore. So while as a feminist I vocally support anyone doing what they want and reject traditional gender roles, in terms of my own negotiation of gender I'm very middle of the road.

Oh. And I should add that in a very basic introductory sense, it's important to note that biological sex isn't a simple matter. I don't have androgenic sexual dimorphisms anymore; I have estrogenic ones. I look female because my body has run on estrogen for years and that's what controls secondary sexual characteristics. Beyond that, if I were treated as medically male, I could die; endocrine balance affects everything from reference ranges for hormone balance (so like, I'm now mildly anemic and need to moderate my diet accordingly, and a close friend needed thyroid medication because estrogenic bodies are dramatically more prone to hypothyroidism, though her doctor didn't catch it at first because he was using male reference ranges), disease symptoms, drug dosing, and so on. I'm not treated as socially male because people "sex" my body, as you put it, and see obviously female (but come on, they also gender bodies, and wearing normative women's clothes and hairstyle works the same way it works for other women--where does sexing the body end and gendering it begin?). 

So the sex/gender dichotomy isn't actually very useful for understanding me as you apply it. Both of those line up very neatly for me, and yet diametrically opposite to the way I was assigned at birth. It doesn't really matter if people are sexing or gendering me; they perceive me straightforwardly as either female or a woman depending on whether you think I'm being sexed or gendered.

Things are more complicated when people aren't clearly binary, but I'd argue that's no reason for treating them less courteously than people who intelligibly fit in the normative boxes. If someone identifies as neither male nor female, that's good enough for me. They can show me what that means to them in their own time if we're friends; until then, I can suspend interacting with them using gendered social scripts.

That's not an unreasonable request, and might be more narrowly accurate on technical grounds, but we're also a marginalized and misunderstood group who face significant opportunity costs for changing terminology. There's a history to our terminology which comes out of the liberation movement rather than philosophical precision.
